courses.title: CARSI Fire & Smoke Restoration Practitioner
courses.description:
An Australian-produced credential course for restoration technicians and supervisors in Australia and New Zealand who respond to fire and smoke damage, and for cleaners, estimators and insurance-support staff who need to understand how a fire job is assessed, run and documented. It builds sound field judgement — it is no substitute for a technician’s own certification, a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet, or a site’s own rules, and it does not license anyone to remove asbestos.

Six modules follow a fire job in the order it happens: the restoration arc with make-safe first; how fire makes smoke and soot and how they travel through a building; the hazardous materials a fire exposes — asbestos, lead paint, silica dust and treated-timber ash — with the Australian and New Zealand rules for each; residue identification, source removal and cleaning; corrosion urgency, contents and the HVAC system; and odour control, verification and the job file, including the Australian and New Zealand insurance and consumer-law context. Every figure is metric, every power reference assumes 230 V / 50 Hz mains, and the regulators cited are Safe Work Australia, the state and territory regulators and WorkSafe New Zealand. Each module ends with a check, a final knowledge check closes the course, and a practical task assesses a whole job.

CARSI Fire & Smoke Restoration Practitioner is a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. Standards are referenced by name only (aligned to the principles of ANSI/IICRC S700:2025); no standard text is reproduced.

modules.title: Module 1: Course Objectives & the Fire Restoration Arc

lessons.title: What this course covers and who it is for
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario and figures are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

A strata manager in Wollongong rings at 7 am. A kitchen fire in a ground-floor unit was put out overnight. The fire brigade has gone, the owner wants the unit cleaned before the tenants come back, and residents on the two floors above say their units smell of smoke. On the same morning a property manager in Hamilton, New Zealand, rings a restorer about almost the same job: a kitchen fire in a 1970s rental, smoke through the house, and an anxious landlord. The building science is the same in both places. The law that governs the work is not, and a practitioner who works on both sides of the Tasman has to know where the two differ.

The idea

This is the credential course for the CARSI Fire & Smoke Restoration Practitioner, a CARSI Southern Hemisphere Restoration Designation. CARSI has no separate Level 2 fire course, so this course both teaches the discipline and assesses it: six teaching modules, a check at the end of each, a final knowledge check and a practical task. The optional foundation course is CARSI Asbestos Awareness for Restoration; it is strongly recommended because asbestos is the hazard most likely to stop a fire job.

The course is written for restoration technicians and supervisors, and for cleaners, estimators and insurance-support staff who need to understand how a fire job is assessed, run and documented. It covers Australia and New Zealand. In Australia the model Work Health and Safety laws apply in every jurisdiction except Victoria, where the Occupational Health and Safety Act 2004 applies and WorkSafe Victoria regulates. In New Zealand the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) applies and WorkSafe New Zealand regulates. Both systems put the primary duty on the person conducting a business or undertaking (PCBU). Where a threshold, licence or notification rule differs between the two countries, the lesson states both. Where nothing differs — AS/NZS standards, 230 V mains, metric units — one statement covers both.

The course is aligned to the principles of ANSI/IICRC S700:2025, the first edition of that standard, cited by name only. No standard text is reproduced, and nothing here should be read as a summary of what the standard says: read your own licensed copy for that. Every other claim in the course is tied to a public source, mostly Australian and New Zealand regulators, and listed at the end of each lesson.

Six modules build the job in the order it happens: (1) the course and the restoration arc, with make-safe first; (2) how fire makes smoke and soot and how they travel through a building; (3) the hazardous materials a fire exposes — asbestos, lead paint, silica dust and treated-timber ash — with the Australian and New Zealand rules for each; (4) identifying the residue and choosing a cleaning method; (5) corrosion urgency, contents and the HVAC system; and (6) odour control, verification and the job file.

Two limits matter from day one. This course does not license you to remove asbestos: in both countries friable asbestos, which includes fire-damaged asbestos, is Class A licensed work. And it does not replace a manufacturer’s instructions, a Safety Data Sheet (SDS) or a site’s own rules.

Four jobs you will meet in this course

The lessons keep coming back to four kinds of job, because each one tests a different part of the method:

  • The house fire — a fire contained in one room of a home, with smoke through the rest of it (Geelong, Ballarat, Christchurch, Palmerston North). The test is the whole-building survey and the hazardous-materials check.
  • The kitchen fire — a pot or appliance fire, often in a rental or a strata unit (Wollongong, Newcastle, Hamilton). Little visible soot, a protein film and a strong odour; the test is reading the residue and dealing with the people in the units around it.
  • The bushfire-affected building — a house or business the fire front did not destroy, but which sits in ash fall, smoke and debris from buildings that burnt nearby. The test is site release, asbestos in a neighbour’s debris, and the ash itself.
  • The commercial job — a café, office or commercial kitchen (Fremantle, Parramatta, Townsville), where an asbestos register should exist, electronics and stock are at stake, and every day of closure costs the business.

Where the bushfire material comes from. Everything this course teaches about bushfire ash and asbestos in bushfire-affected buildings is drawn from Australian and New Zealand regulators and health authorities, named in each lesson. Read the bushfire sections as regulator guidance only: CARSI claims its nominative alignment to the principles of S700:2025 for the restoration method taught in the other sections, not for the bushfire material.

How you earn the designation. Pass each of the six module checks, the final knowledge check and the practical task, each at 80 % or higher. Every question explains its answer, so a wrong answer still teaches you something.

See it

The roadmap shows the six modules in job order, with the hazardous-materials module placed before any cleaning, because that is where it sits on site.

Do it in metric

Size the Wollongong loss before anyone quotes it. The kitchen is 3.6 m × 3.0 m, so 10.8 m² of floor; at a 2.4 m ceiling that is about 25.9 m³ of air. Smoke also reached the hall (6.0 m × 1.2 m = 7.2 m²) and the lounge (4.5 m × 4.0 m = 18.0 m²). The affected floor area is 10.8 + 7.2 + 18.0 = 36.0 m² in this unit alone, before you have looked at the units above. Record each room separately: a single “whole unit” figure hides where the residue is heaviest.

Field download

The Fire first-attendance card lists the make-safe checks, the Australian and New Zealand contacts, and the first measurements to record, room by room.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks who holds the primary duty, which law applies in Victoria and in New Zealand, and how to size a loss in square metres. Each answer explains the reasoning.

Takeaway

One discipline, two legal systems. Know which law applies where you are working, size the loss room by room in square metres, and treat the hazardous-materials check as part of the assessment, not an afterthought. Next lesson: the restoration arc and why make-safe comes first.

lessons.title: The fire restoration arc: make safe first
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Equipment current draws and timings are illustrative and flagged for verification.

On the job

You arrive at a fire-damaged house in Geelong at 9 am. The power is off at the meter box, the ceiling over the kitchen sags, and the owner has already started wiping soot off the benchtop with a wet cloth. Your apprentice wants to plug in an air scrubber and start. Everything about the next hour is decided by the order you do things in.

The idea

A fire job runs along an arc: make safe → assess → mitigate → remove the source → clean → control odour → verify → document. Documentation runs the whole way through, not just at the end. The order matters because each step changes what the next one finds. Cleaning before the hazardous-materials check can spread asbestos fibres or lead dust; deodorising before the source is removed only masks the smell; and closing up a wall cavity before it is dry and clean traps both moisture and odour.

Make safe comes first, and it is a legal duty, not a preference. Under the model WHS laws a PCBU has the primary duty of care for workers and must eliminate risks so far as is reasonably practicable, and if that is not reasonably practicable, minimise them. New Zealand’s HSWA puts the same primary duty on the PCBU. Make-safe on a fire job means:

  • Site control. Confirm with whoever controls the site (the fire service, police or the owner) that it has been released to you. A fire scene may be under investigation.
  • Structure. A sagging or water-loaded ceiling and fire-weakened framing can fail. Do not work under them; get an engineer or builder to make them safe.
  • Power. Fire damages wiring in ways you cannot see. Leave restoration of supply to a licensed electrician. Run your own equipment through a residual current device (RCD). In Australia, WorkSafe ACT states that portable electrical equipment, power tools and extension leads at a workplace must be protected by an RCD (check your own state or territory regulator), and in-service equipment is inspected and tested under AS/NZS 3760:2022. In New Zealand, WorkSafe says electrical equipment on construction sites should be RCD-protected and that the Electricity (Safety) Regulations require RCD protection in damp conditions. NZ law does not require testing and tagging, although AS/NZS 3760 is one way to show equipment is safe.
  • Hazardous materials. Check for asbestos, lead paint and treated-timber ash before anything is disturbed (Module 3).
  • People. Fit-tested respirators for anyone entering (Module 3), and occupants kept out of the work area.

If someone is seriously hurt, or a dangerous incident occurs, the notification duty applies. In Australia a PCBU must notify the WHS regulator immediately and preserve the site until an inspector arrives or directs otherwise. In New Zealand a PCBU must notify WorkSafe as soon as possible, by the fastest means available, and keep a record of the event for at least five years.

Field walk-through: the first 30 minutes in Geelong

Walk the Geelong job as a series of decisions, in the order they arrive.

  1. At the kerb. Before you get out of the van, ring whoever released the site and record who it was and when. If the fire service or police still control it, you wait.
  2. At the front door. The owner is wiping soot with a wet cloth. Stop it politely and explain why: wet-wiping dry soot smears it into the surface, and until the hazardous-materials check is done nobody should be disturbing residue without a respirator. Ask when the house was built and whether it has been renovated; that answer starts the asbestos and lead questions in Module 3.
  3. In the kitchen doorway. The sagging ceiling decides where anyone can stand. Nobody works under it. Photograph it from the doorway and call a builder or engineer to make it safe.
  4. At the meter box. The power is off, and it stays off until a licensed electrician says otherwise. Your air scrubber waits for a circuit the electrician has confirmed, and it runs through an RCD.
  5. Back at the van. Now open the job file properly: who released the site, the make-safe actions, the first photos, and the hazards still open.

Common mistakes on day one

  • Starting work because the owner is anxious. The urgency is real; it does not move the make-safe steps.
  • Plugging into the nearest outlet because “the lights work next door”. A fire-affected circuit is the electrician’s call.
  • Leaving the job file until the end of the day. The make-safe record is the first thing an insurer or a regulator will ask for if anything goes wrong.

See it

The arc runs left to right with the job file underneath it, because every step adds to the file.

Do it in metric

Before the apprentice plugs in, do the power budget at 230 V. Australian mains is nominally 230 V, and so is New Zealand’s. Suppose (illustrative figures: read your own rating plates) the air scrubber draws 2.5 A and the HEPA vacuum 4.3 A. Together that is 6.8 A, or 230 × 6.8 ≈ 1,564 W, on a 10 A circuit, leaving 3.2 A. Add a dehumidifier drawing 3.9 A and the circuit would carry 10.7 A — over its rating — so the dehumidifier goes on a second circuit, and only once an electrician has confirmed that circuit is safe to use after the fire.

Field download

The Fire first-attendance card walks the make-safe checks in order, with a 230 V power budget box and the notification contacts for Australia and New Zealand.

Check yourself

The Module 1 check asks you to put the arc in order, explain why cleaning cannot come before the hazardous-materials check, and complete a 230 V power budget.

Takeaway

Make safe, then assess, and only then start work. Keep the job file running from the first minute. Next module: how fire makes smoke and soot, and where they go.

lessons.title: How fire makes smoke and soot
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Descriptions of how residue forms are flagged for SME verification.

On the job

Two fires in the same week. In a Ballarat house a heater ignited curtains and the room flashed over in minutes: black, dry, powdery soot sits on every ceiling. In a Wellington flat a cigarette smouldered in a couch for hours before the alarm sounded: there is far less visible soot, but a sticky brown film on the windows and a smell that makes your eyes water. Same fuel load, very different jobs. How the fire burned tells you what you are about to clean.

The idea

Fire is a chemical reaction that rarely burns its fuel completely. Incomplete combustion leaves fine particles (soot), partly burnt organic compounds, water vapour and gases. Smoke from fires is made up of gases, water vapour and coarse and fine particles of ash, described by size: PM10 particles are smaller than 10 microns, and PM2.5 particles are smaller than 2.5 microns — too small to see, and small enough, when breathed in, to go deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. That is why fire residue is a health hazard as well as a cleaning problem, and why smoke can linger inside buildings long after the flames are out.

In CARSI’s teaching, two broad burn conditions are the first clue to the residue:

  • Fast, hot, flaming fires with plenty of air tend to leave a drier, more powdery residue.
  • Slow, low-oxygen, smouldering fires, often involving foams, plastics and furnishings, tend to leave a wetter, smeary residue with a stronger smell.

Treat that as a starting hypothesis, not a diagnosis: Module 4 shows how to test the residue on each surface before you choose a cleaning method. What burned matters as much as how. Synthetic materials such as PVC give off acid gases when they burn; Module 5 deals with the corrosion that follows.

Two consequences follow for the technician. First, protect yourself before you disturb residue: wiping, brushing and demolition put fine particles back into the air you breathe. Bushfire smoke guidance from Australian health authorities recommends P2/N95 masks, and CARSI applies the same logic indoors: a fit-tested P2 respirator as the minimum for residue work, more where the hazard assessment says so. Second, protect the occupants: anyone with asthma, heart or lung disease, older people, pregnant women and young children are the groups health authorities identify as more at risk from smoke.

Worked scenario: the bushfire-affected house that did not burn

(Illustrative.) A weatherboard house near Cobargo, NSW, survived a bushfire front that destroyed two houses further along the road. Nothing in it burnt. For two days it sat in heavy smoke with the windows shut while the owners ran the roof-mounted evaporative cooler to stay cool. Fine grey ash lies on every windowsill, the ceiling around each cooler outlet is shadowed, and the whole house smells of smoke.

This is not a structure fire, and the residue says so: fine, dry ash and smoke particles carried in from outside, not a film from materials burning in the room. EPA Victoria notes that even with doors and windows closed and heating or cooling turned off, ash can still get in, through cracked cornices, unsealed fans and vents, gaps in ceiling roses and around doors and windows. Here the cooler made it far worse. Australian health authorities advise against running evaporative coolers in smoke because they bring outside air inside, and Victoria’s Better Health Channel says a cooler in use can replace all the air in a house every 2 to 3 minutes.

Do the numbers. The house has 180 m² of floor under a 2.4 m ceiling: about 432 m³ of air. One complete change every 3 minutes is 20 changes an hour, or about 8,640 m³ of smoky outside air pushed through the house every hour the cooler ran. That is a whole-house deposit, so this job is surveyed and scoped as a whole house, ducts included (Module 5).

Decision point. The owners have a young child with asthma. Young children and people with lung conditions are among the groups health authorities identify as more at risk from smoke, so the family stays out while residue is being disturbed, and the cooler stays off until its system has been assessed and cleaned.

See it

The diagram pairs each burn condition with the residue it tends to leave, and shows how small PM10 and PM2.5 particles are.

Do it in metric

Put the particle sizes in units you can picture. One micron is one thousandth of a millimetre, so a PM2.5 particle is under 0.0025 mm across and a PM10 particle under 0.01 mm. The Ballarat lounge is 4.2 m × 3.8 m with a 2.4 m ceiling: 16.0 m² of floor and about 38.3 m³ of air. Every cubic metre of that air was full of particles during the fire, and particles this small settle slowly and travel on the slightest draught, which is why you survey the whole building and not just the burnt room (next lesson).

Field download

The Smoke migration survey sheet has a column for the burn condition you infer in each room, and for the evidence behind it: residue texture, smell and what burned.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks what PM2.5 means and why it matters, and how burn conditions shape the residue you expect.

Takeaway

How it burned and what burned set the residue. Fine particles are a health hazard, so protect yourself and the occupants before you disturb anything. Next lesson: how smoke gets into rooms the fire never reached.

Sources for this lesson

  • Australian Government Department of Health, Bushfire smoke: general information. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Australian Centre for Disease Control, Staying safe from bushfire smoke. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Cider L. Reconditioning surface mount electronics after smoke contamination. IVF report 92/20, 1992 (NIST FireDOC abstract). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Better Health Channel (Victorian Department of Health), Using air conditioners when it’s smoky outside. Read 02/11/2026.
  • EPA Victoria, Ash and soot from fires: fact sheet 1724.1 (February 2020). Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: How smoke travels through a building
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Migration pathways are CARSI method and flagged for SME verification.

On the job

A two-storey house in Christchurch had a fire in the downstairs laundry. The laundry and hall are black. Upstairs, the owner says, “is fine, it just smells a bit.” You go upstairs and find a grey line of soot along the top of each bedroom door, and the ceiling around the downlights is shadowed. Smoke has been everywhere; it just has not been everywhere equally.

The idea

In CARSI’s method, smoke and soot move through a building by five pathways, and a proper assessment checks each one:

  • Heat and buoyancy. Hot smoke rises, spreads across the ceiling, then cools and moves outward and down.
  • Stack effect. Warm, smoke-laden air rises through stairwells, service risers, wall cavities and roof spaces, carrying smoke to upper floors and the roof void even when the fire was low in the building.
  • Pressure and air movement. Open doors, broken windows, gaps under doors and around downlights let smoke follow the air. A ducted heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) system that ran during or after the fire can carry residue to every room it serves (Module 5).
  • Cool surfaces. Residue tends to deposit where moving air meets cooler surfaces: external walls, window frames, the tops of door openings.
  • Porous materials. Carpet, upholstery, plasterboard and timber absorb odour-causing compounds, so a room can smell strongly while showing little soot.

The working rule is simple: assess the whole building, including roof space, wall cavities, ductwork and adjoining units, not just the visibly burnt area. In strata buildings and terraces this extends to the units either side and above, which may need their own assessment and their own owner’s authority. Missing a pathway is how a job looks clean at handover and smells of smoke three weeks later.

Use the survey to set a boundary: the line between affected and unaffected areas, recorded on a sketch with what you saw, smelt and measured. That boundary drives the scope, the quote and the cleaning plan, and it is the first thing an insurer’s assessor will ask to see.

Worked scenario: the café under the apartments

(Illustrative.) A fire in the back room of a ground-floor café in a three-storey mixed-use building in Fremantle, WA, is put out by firefighters within twenty minutes. The café is heavily sooted. Above it are six apartments and a shared stairwell. The building manager wants the café trading again by the weekend and says the apartments “only smell a bit”.

Walk the five pathways against the whole building, not just the café:

  • Stack effect: the stairwell and the service risers for plumbing and cabling run from the café ceiling to the roof. Check the landings and riser cupboards on every floor.
  • Pressure and air movement: the café’s kitchen exhaust and any shared mechanical ventilation can push smoke into common areas. Ask what was running during the fire.
  • Cool surfaces: look for shadow lines at apartment door heads, around downlights and on window frames on the side of the building the smoke rose up.
  • Porous materials: corridor carpet and apartment soft furnishings can smell strongly with no visible soot.

Decision points. Each apartment has its own owner or tenancy, and the stairwell and corridors are common property controlled by the strata company or owners corporation. Your authority to survey and scope comes from each of them, not from the café owner. On a commercial building, ask for the asbestos register before anything is disturbed (Module 3). Then set the boundary floor by floor on the sketch: “café, stairwell, apartments 1 and 2” is a scope an insurer can follow; “whole building, light smoke” is not.

Common mistake. Scoping the visibly burnt tenancy and leaving the rest for later. By the time the apartment owners complain, the residue has aged, the claim has split in two, and nobody can show where the smoke went.

See it

The five numbered cards set out each pathway and where its residue tends to show up, ending with the whole-building survey and the boundary.

Do it in metric

Work out how much opening the smoke had. Each bedroom door upstairs has a 10 mm gap under an 820 mm leaf: 10 × 820 = 8,200 mm², or 0.0082 m². Five doors give about 0.041 m² of open gap — roughly the area of a 200 mm × 200 mm hole. The stairwell rises 5.2 m. A small opening and a tall warm column are all smoke needs, which is why the shadow lines sit at the door heads.

Field download

The Smoke migration survey sheet lists the five pathways as a checklist for each room, with a sketch grid for the boundary and space for the evidence at each point.

Check yourself

The Module 2 check asks you to name the pathways, explain why an upstairs room can smell strongly with little soot, and decide where the boundary of a job lies.

Takeaway

Smoke goes where the air goes. Survey the whole building, draw the boundary, and record the evidence for it. Next module: what a fire exposes that is more dangerous than soot.

lessons.title: Asbestos in fire-damaged buildings: Australia and New Zealand
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario figures are illustrative. Regulatory statements are sourced; check your state, territory or WorkSafe NZ guidance for the job.

On the job

A 1972 brick-veneer house in Toowoomba lost its kitchen and back verandah to fire. Pieces of grey sheet lie among the charred timber under the eaves, and some have shattered into small fragments across the lawn. The owner wants you to “just clear the debris so we can see what’s left.” In Dunedin, a 1960s weatherboard villa has a similar fire, with cracked fibre-cement soffits. Neither job can start the way the owner wants.

The idea

When was it built or renovated? In Australia, assume asbestos may be present in any building built or renovated before 31 December 2003, when the national ban took effect. Buildings built or renovated before 1990 are the most likely to contain it. Workplaces in buildings built before 31 December 2003 must have an asbestos register (in Queensland, before 31 December 1989; Victoria sets its own register rules), so ask for it on commercial jobs. In New Zealand, any building built or renovated before 2000 could contain asbestos (WorkSafe NZ). A later build date never proves a building is asbestos-free, and you cannot tell whether a material contains asbestos by looking at it.

What did the fire do to it? Heat can crack, break or shatter asbestos-containing materials and release fibres, and the fibres often stay in the ash and debris. Shattered fibre-cement can be thrown well beyond where it started, sometimes past the property boundary. Fire changes the legal category of the material:

  • New South Wales: the NSW EPA guidance on asbestos in bushfires says asbestos-containing material directly impacted by fire is considered friable, and that all fire-damaged asbestos removal must be done by Class A licensed removalists.
  • Victoria: WorkSafe Victoria says fire-damaged non-friable material should either be assumed to have become friable (Class A removal) or be thoroughly inspected by a competent person as part of the site risk assessment.
  • New Zealand: WorkSafe’s removal guidance says a non-friable source damaged by an event such as fire should be reclassified as friable, and its removal, and the dust and debris it produced, must be done by a Class A removalist.

The licence classes line up across the Tasman. In both countries a Class A licence covers friable asbestos and any amount of asbestos-contaminated dust and debris; a Class B licence covers non-friable asbestos; and without a licence a person may remove only up to 10 m² of non-friable material (in the ACT, any removal needs a licence). In New Zealand the 10 m² is counted cumulatively over the whole removal project for the site, and WorkSafe says a large area cannot be divided into smaller sectors to get around it. The 10 m² exemption is irrelevant once fire has made the material friable.

What the restorer does: stop, do not disturb the material, keep people out, and hand the affected area to a licensed asbestos assessor and Class A removalist. Authorities may keep debris damp with a fine mist or a PVA bonding agent until removal. Restoration cleaning in that area starts only after clearance. In New Zealand, a licensed removalist who starts emergency removal after a sudden event such as a fire must notify WorkSafe immediately by phone and in writing within 24 hours.

Worked scenario: asbestos next door after a bushfire

(Illustrative.) After a bushfire in the Blue Mountains, NSW, a 1998 brick house is standing, with smoke damage and a scorched timber deck. The 1960s fibro cottage next door burnt to the ground, and pieces of broken grey sheet lie across your client’s lawn and along the shared fence. The insurer wants smoke cleaning to start this week. Work through it in order.

  1. Is the site released? The NSW EPA says not to enter a property after a bushfire until emergency services or the local council confirm it is safe. Bushfire sites add hazards of their own: SafeWork NSW warns of downed live power lines, active solar panels, and hot coals hidden under rubble.
  2. Whose asbestos is it? The fragments came from next door, but they are on your client’s land and in your work area. Treat every fragment as fire-damaged, and therefore friable: Class A work. Your client’s own house was built in 1998, before the 2003 ban, so its materials are suspect too, even though it is younger than the most likely pre-1990 period.
  3. What is already in place? Depending on the scale of the fire, NSW Public Works, the EPA or the council may assess fire-affected properties and put controls in place: fencing, warning signs, and debris kept damp with a fine mist or PVA. The NSW EPA also says clean-up may start with a safety assessment of nearby properties, so fibres are not spread during the work. Do not disturb those controls.
  4. What can your crew do? Nothing in the fragment field until a licensed assessor and a Class A removalist have dealt with it and the area is cleared. Indoor smoke cleaning can be planned, but the route in and out of the house must not cross the debris.

In Victoria, WorkSafe adds a precautionary rule for bushfire sites: where fire-affected asbestos cannot be reached to be inspected, it is treated as friable and a Class A licence holder must be engaged. Only where a competent person finds the material has stayed non-friable, for example where the fire damaged the area around a building but left the building itself with minimal damage, may a Class B holder do the removal. Samples go to a NATA-accredited laboratory. The Victorian Government may also appoint its own clean-up contractor for bushfire-destroyed properties, so ask who is managing the site before you quote.

In New Zealand, WorkSafe notes that damaged asbestos-containing materials are less dangerous while wet but can release fibres once they dry, and that a licensed asbestos assessor or removalist should be contacted before a building presumed to contain asbestos is reoccupied. The pre-2000 build-date rule applies to a building damaged by a vegetation fire exactly as it does to a house fire.

Common mistakes on bushfire jobs

  • Sweeping or blowing ash off paths and decks. The NSW EPA says not to use a broom, and EPA Victoria says not to use leaf blowers or anything that pushes ash into the air.
  • Hosing debris down hard. Dampen it, but the NSW EPA says not to use high-pressure water, and SafeWork NSW warns that dust suppression should not be so heavy that it runs off into drains and waterways.
  • Burying rubble or ash on site. Building rubble should not be buried, because it may contain hazardous materials.
  • Leaving the site in your PPE. Take it off before you leave, put it in a heavy-duty 0.2 mm plastic bag, seal it, and dispose of it as asbestos waste.

See it

The decision flow puts the build-date question first and sends any fire-damaged suspect material straight to the licensed process.

Do it in metric

The Toowoomba house was built in 1972, well before the 2003 ban and inside the most likely period. Its eaves lining is 0.45 m deep and runs 18 m along the back of the house: 0.45 × 18 = 8.1 m². Undamaged and non-friable, 8.1 m² would sit under the 10 m² unlicensed limit. Fire-damaged, it is treated as friable, so the area no longer matters: it is Class A work whatever its size. Record the area, the build year (1972) and the condition in the job file, and mark the fragment field on your sketch in metres from the house.

Field download

The Australia and New Zealand hazardous-materials card sets the asbestos questions, licence classes and contacts for both countries side by side.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks for the build-date thresholds in each country, why the 10 m² rule stops applying after a fire, and what the restorer does on finding suspect debris.

Takeaway

Built or renovated before the 2003 ban in Australia (most likely before 1990), or before 2000 in New Zealand: suspect asbestos. Fire-damaged asbestos is friable and is Class A work in both countries. Stop, isolate, hand over. Next lesson: lead, silica and treated-timber ash.

lessons.title: Lead paint, silica dust and treated-timber ash
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Scenario figures are illustrative. Regulatory statements are sourced.

On the job

After a garage fire at a 1950s house in Adelaide, the scope includes stripping fire-blistered paint from the eaves and fascia, cutting out a cracked concrete hob, and clearing the ash where a timber pergola and paling fence burnt. A crew in Tauranga has nearly the same scope after a carport fire. Three more hazards hide in that list, and each has rules that differ between the two countries.

The idea

Lead paint. In Australia, paint containing lead was used in many homes before 1970, and homes built more recently may still have it. In New Zealand, if a building was built in the 1980s or earlier, WorkSafe and Health New Zealand say it is best to presume it has been painted with lead-based paint. You cannot identify lead paint by looking at it. A fire can blister and char lead paint, and fire and demolition open ceiling cavities where lead dust may have built up for decades. Heat is the specific danger: NSW guidance warns that open-flame torches on lead paint create lead fumes. On a fire job, test or presume, do not dry-sand or dry-sweep, use a HEPA vacuum and wet wiping, and keep pregnant women and young children away.

Silica dust. Respirable crystalline silica (RCS) comes from cutting, grinding, drilling or breaking concrete, brick, stone, mortar and fibre-cement. Demolition and make-safe on a fire job produce it. The exposure limits differ:

  • Australia: the workplace exposure standard for RCS is 0.05 mg/m³ as an eight-hour time-weighted average, and it must not be exceeded. Australia moves to Workplace Exposure Limits on 1 December 2026, and the RCS value stays the same at that switch.
  • New Zealand: WorkSafe lowered the RCS workplace exposure standard to 0.025 mg/m³ in November 2023. New Zealand WES are generally advisory rather than mandatory, which MBIE contrasts with Australia, where all WES are mandatory. Advisory does not mean optional: the HSWA duty to eliminate or minimise risk still applies.

Control silica at the source: wet cutting and on-tool extraction first, then respiratory protection that complies with AS/NZS 1716, selected under AS/NZS 1715 and fit-tested to the wearer.

Treated-timber ash. Fences, pergolas, decks and poles are often copper chrome arsenate (CCA) treated pine. Queensland Health and EPA Victoria advise treating ash from burnt CCA timber as containing copper, chromium and arsenic, because you cannot tell by looking, and they say the ash and char can contain up to 10 % of those metals by weight. Moisten the ash, shovel it rather than sweep it, do not use high-pressure water, double-bag it and take it to landfill as your council directs; never bury it or put it in a garden or organics bin. A question-and-answer sheet published by New Zealand’s EPA (prepared by its predecessor, ERMA) advises not burning CCA-treated wood because toxic chemicals may be released in the smoke and ashes, so treat NZ fire ash from treated timber the same way and check your regional or district council for disposal.

Respirators, both countries. A tight-fitting respirator is fit-tested before first use and fit-checked every time it goes on. Facial hair under the seal stops it sealing; where that is the case, use a respirator that does not rely on a face seal, such as a hood-type powered respirator.

Worked scenario: the fence line after a grassfire

(Illustrative.) A grassfire on the edge of Toowoomba burns 40 m of treated-pine paling fence and a pergola behind a 1984 house before firefighters stop it at the patio. The rear walls are smoke-stained, the fascia paint has blistered, and ash covers the patio and lawn. SafeWork NSW lists what bushfire debris can hold: asbestos, ash from burnt CCA-treated timber, medicines, garden and household chemicals, damaged gas bottles, and metal residues from burnt appliances. On this job the fence and pergola ash is the hazard you can see; the others are the ones you check for.

Decision points.

  • The ash. Treat the paling and pergola ash as CCA ash unless shown otherwise: moisten it, shovel it, double-bag it and take it to landfill as the council directs. Never spread it on the garden or put it in the organics bin.
  • The paint. A 1984 house is younger than the 1970 lead-paint flag in Australia, but newer homes may still have lead paint, so the blistered fascia is tested before anyone strips it, and never with an open flame. The same house in New Zealand would be presumed to have lead-based paint.
  • The eaves. If the eaves are fibre-cement, a 1984 build sits inside the most likely period for asbestos; any that are cracked or scorched go through the Module 3 process before the paint work starts.

Common mistakes with ash

  • Blowing or sweeping ash off the patio. It puts fine particles, and any metals or fibres, back into the air. Dampen it and shovel it.
  • Washing ash into the garden beds or the stormwater drain.
  • Assuming a newer house means no hazards. The fence, the shed and the neighbour’s building may all be older than the house.
  • Wearing a paper dust mask. SafeWork NSW says ordinary paper dust masks, handkerchiefs and bandannas should not be used, and that P2 masks are the minimum for fine particles, including asbestos fibres.

See it

The table sets each hazard’s Australian and New Zealand position side by side, so a crew that works both countries can see where the numbers change.

Do it in metric

Two calculations. Silica: the New Zealand standard of 0.025 mg/m³ is half the Australian 0.05 mg/m³, so a cutting method that keeps an Australian crew at 0.04 mg/m³ is under the Australian standard but above the New Zealand one. CCA ash: the pergola and fence leave about 20 kg of ash and char. At up to 10 % metals by weight, that is up to 2 kg of copper, chromium and arsenic compounds — which is why it is bagged, labelled and taken to landfill, not spread on the garden.

Field download

The Australia and New Zealand hazardous-materials card carries the lead, silica and ash rules for both countries, plus Poisons Information on 13 11 26 (Australia) and the National Poisons Centre on 0800 764 766 (New Zealand), with 000 and 111 for emergencies.

Check yourself

The Module 3 check asks for the lead-paint date flags in each country, the two silica standards, and how to handle CCA ash.

Takeaway

Presume lead in older paint, control silica at the source, and treat treated-timber ash as toxic. The New Zealand silica number is half the Australian one. Next module: reading the residue and choosing how to clean it.

lessons.title: Reading the residue: types and the test patch
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Residue categories and test methods are CARSI method wording flagged for SME verification against field practice and the licensed standard.

On the job

A Newcastle house had a pot left on the stove all afternoon. There is almost no black soot, but every painted surface in the kitchen and lounge has a faint yellow film, and the smell is overwhelming. Next door, a heater fault put an oily, dark film through the ducted system. The apprentice wants to use the same cleaner on both. The residue on each surface decides the method, so you identify it first, room by room.

The idea

CARSI teaches four working residue types. They are field labels to guide the first test, not a diagnosis:

  • Dry smoke residue — from a fast, hot fire of natural materials. Powdery, smears little, usually the easiest to remove.
  • Wet smoke residue — from a slow, smouldering, low-oxygen fire, often of plastics and foams. Sticky and smeary, with a strong smell. Wiping it the wrong way pushes it into porous surfaces.
  • Protein residue — from cooking fires and burnt food. A thin, near-invisible yellowish film that discolours paint and varnish, with an odour out of all proportion to what you can see.
  • Fuel-oil residue — from oil-fired heaters and equipment faults rather than a structure fire. Oily, dark, with a distinct smell, and it travels well through ductwork.

One job can show more than one type, so record the type for each room and surface, not one label for the whole house.

The test patch. Before choosing a method, test it on a small, inconspicuous area of each surface type: painted plasterboard, gloss timber, glass, fabric, stone. Start with the least aggressive method that might work and step up only if it fails. Record what you tried, what happened, and a photo before and after. The test patch protects the substrate — the paint, the finish, the fabric — and it protects you when an owner later asks why a wall needed repainting.

Surfaces and age. Residue changes with time. Acidic residue keeps working on finishes and metals (Module 5), and odour compounds keep migrating into porous materials. A residue tested on day one may behave differently on day ten, so date every test.

Standards. This course is aligned to the principles of ANSI/IICRC S700:2025, cited by name only. How the standard itself classifies residues and assessment is a matter for your licensed copy; CARSI’s four labels are teaching categories.

Field walk-through: the rental kitchen in Newcastle

(Illustrative.) Walk the Newcastle kitchen with the test-patch log in hand.

  1. Look, then touch with a gloved fingertip on a hidden spot. No black powder comes away, but the glove picks up a faint yellow tack, and the odour is strong. Working label: protein residue.
  2. Check the next room. The lounge shows the same film, thinner. Same label, lighter loading: record it separately.
  3. Check next door. The neighbour’s unit, with the faulty heater, has an oily dark film around its outlets. Different source, different label: fuel-oil residue. That is a separate job file, with that owner’s authority.
  4. Test, gentlest first. On the painted plasterboard, a dry sponge does little to a protein film. That is the expected result, and you record it. Step up to a method the product label and SDS allow for protein films, on the 100 mm × 100 mm patch only.
  5. Look again when it is dry. A patch that looks clean while wet can dry with a ring or a change in gloss. That is a fail, and it goes in the log as one.

Common mistakes

  • One label for the whole house. A kitchen can carry protein residue while the lounge beside it carries dry soot from a different fire event.
  • Testing in the middle of a wall. Pick a low, hidden spot, so a failed patch is easy to repaint.
  • Judging a patch while it is still wet.
  • Not dating the test. Residue keeps changing, so an undated test cannot be compared with one done a week later.

See it

The four cards give each residue’s usual source, look and feel, and the clue that separates it from the others.

Do it in metric

Plan the tests for the Newcastle kitchen and lounge. You have four surface types (painted plasterboard, painted timber trim, glass, upholstery) in two rooms, so eight test patches. Keep each patch to about 100 mm × 100 mm (0.01 m²) in a low, hidden spot. Eight patches total 0.08 m² — trivial to repaint if a test fails, and enough to choose a method for the 46 m² of wall and ceiling still to clean.

Field download

The Residue test and cleaning card has a test-patch log: room, surface, residue type, method tried, result and photo reference.

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to identify residue types from site descriptions and to explain the purpose of a test patch.

Takeaway

Identify the residue on each surface, test before you clean, start gentle, and write down what happened. Next lesson: choosing and sequencing the cleaning.

Sources for this lesson

  • Liu X et al. Corrosive effects of smoke with different concentrations from PVC on 304 stainless steel and 6061 aluminium alloy. Corros Eng Sci Technol 2018. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Source removal and cleaning: method and sequence
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Cleaning methods and sequence are CARSI method wording flagged for SME verification.

On the job

In a Launceston unit the burnt couch, a melted TV and the kitchen’s charred upper cupboards are still in place. A crew member has started wiping the lounge ceiling, and black streaks are spreading. Two things are wrong: the sources of residue and smell are still in the room, and the ceiling has been wiped wet when it carries dry soot.

The idea

Source removal first. Charred, melted and saturated materials keep releasing particles and odour. Remove what cannot be saved — charred timber, collapsed linings, burnt soft furnishings — before you clean what can, and only after the hazardous-materials check (Module 3) has cleared that area. Photograph and inventory contents before anything leaves the site, because it is the record of the claim (Module 5).

Method follows residue. Your test patches (previous lesson) choose the method. As a working guide in CARSI’s method:

  • Dry residue: dry methods first — HEPA vacuuming and dry chemical sponges — before any liquid, because water smears dry soot into the surface.
  • Wet residue: a degreasing cleaner suited to the smeary film, with ventilation and the PPE the SDS calls for.
  • Protein residue: a cleaner designed to break down protein films; expect the odour work (Module 6) to be the bigger job.
  • Fuel-oil residue: a solvent-based degreaser, with particular attention to HVAC and duct surfaces.

Read the Safety Data Sheet for every product and follow its label, in either country. The SDS is your first source for the PPE and ventilation a product needs; if anything on it is unclear, ask the supplier before you use it.

Sequence. Work top-down and clean-to-dirty: ceilings, then walls, then fixtures, then floors, so residue falls onto surfaces you have not cleaned yet. Work from the least affected rooms toward the most affected, so you do not track residue back into finished areas. Keep air filtration running while you clean, to catch what you put into the air.

Wet structure. Firefighting water often leaves the building wet. The drying rules from water restoration apply: measure, set a dry goal and dry to it before closing anything up. If mould is present or develops, do not blow air movers across it; contain it and use air filtration and dehumidification until it has been cleaned and cleared.

Worked scenario: the office floor

(Illustrative.) An electrical fire in a print room on the third floor of a 1985 office building in Parramatta, NSW, leaves dry soot across an open-plan floor of about 600 m², with a suspended grid ceiling of 1,200 mm × 600 mm tiles, carpet tiles and 80 workstations. The tenant wants staff back on Monday.

Decision point 1: the register. A 1985 building was built well before the 2003 ban and inside the most likely period, and as a workplace it must have an asbestos register. Read it before anyone lifts a ceiling tile or opens a riser.

Decision point 2: the sequence. Source first: the print room’s burnt equipment and linings come out after clearance. Then top-down: ceiling tiles (cleaned or replaced, by your test results), the grid, walls and partitions, the workstations, and the carpet tiles last. Work from the far, least affected end of the floor towards the print room, so cleaned zones sit behind you.

Decision point 3: the electronics. Workstations and printers are not cleaned and powered up to “see if they work” (Module 5). They are isolated, labelled and referred.

Do the numbers. One ceiling tile is 1.2 × 0.6 = 0.72 m², so the 600 m² floor holds about 600 ÷ 0.72 ≈ 833 tiles. If your test patches show that a quarter of them, the heavily sooted ones near the print room, cannot be cleaned to a satisfactory result, that is about 208 tiles to replace, or about 150 m² of ceiling. Put the count, the reason and the test record in the scope.

Common mistakes

  • Cleaning the carpet before the ceiling, then cleaning it again.
  • Starting in the burnt room because it looks worst, then tracking soot across the clean end of the floor.
  • Switching off air filtration the moment wiping stops. Fine particles stay in the air long after the work that stirred them up.

See it

The sequence shows why source removal and test patches sit before any wiping, and why work runs top-down.

Do it in metric

Measure the Launceston lounge for the cleaning scope. The room is 4.0 m × 3.4 m with a 2.4 m ceiling. The ceiling is 4.0 × 3.4 = 13.6 m². The walls are the perimeter (2 × (4.0 + 3.4) = 14.8 m) times the height: 14.8 × 2.4 = 35.5 m², less a 2.1 m² window and a 1.7 m² door, so 31.7 m². Ceiling plus walls is 45.3 m² to clean, top-down, ceiling first.

Field download

The Residue test and cleaning card lists the method by residue, the top-down sequence and an area worksheet for ceilings and walls in m².

Check yourself

The Module 4 check asks you to sequence a cleaning job, match a method to a residue, and calculate a wall and ceiling area.

Takeaway

Remove the source, choose the method from the test, and clean top-down from the least affected room. Next module: why metals and electronics cannot wait.

Sources for this lesson

  • Safe Work Australia, Construction duties: asbestos. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Corrosion urgency: why metals and electronics cannot wait
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Timeframes and humidity targets are flagged for SME verification.

On the job

A small commercial kitchen in Townsville had an electrical fire in a switchboard cupboard. The stainless benches, the chrome tapware and a rack of point-of-sale terminals are filmed with grey soot. It is 26 °C and 80 %RH inside. The owner wants to know why you want to wipe the metal today when the insurer has not approved the full scope.

The idea

Smoke attacks metal. Combustion research is clear on the direction, if not the clock. When PVC, which is common in cable insulation, plumbing and furnishings, burns it forms hydrogen chloride, an aggressive acid that deposits on surfaces. Laboratory work has shown smoke from burning PVC causing pitting corrosion on stainless steel and aluminium alloy in high humidity, worsening with exposure time. A broader study exposed steel and copper to smoke from a range of burning materials, held them for 28 days at 75 % relative humidity, and found that all the smokes tested were corrosive, with corrosion depending on the metal, temperature, humidity, exposure time and surface.

Three practical rules follow:

  • Corrosion is time-critical mitigation. Removing residue from exposed metal and electronics is emergency work that comes before the full cleaning scope, not after it. The often-quoted window of the first 24 to 48 hours is CARSI practice wording to be confirmed; the research supports “the sooner the better” and that corrosion gets worse with time.
  • Humidity speeds it up. The studies used high humidity. Bringing the indoor relative humidity down with dehumidification slows corrosion while you work and protects materials, and it is needed anyway if firefighting water has wetted the building.
  • Electronics are a specialist call. Do not power up smoke-contaminated equipment to “see if it works”. Isolate it, document it, and refer it to an electronics restoration specialist or the owner’s service provider. Powering a contaminated board can turn a cleanable item into a loss.

Explain this to the owner and the insurer in plain terms: corrosion control is mitigation that reduces the claim, not an extra. Record when you started and what you did on each item.

Decision points: the first two hours in Townsville

  1. Approval. This course treats corrosion control as emergency mitigation that starts before the full scope is approved. Ring the insurer or its assessor, say what you are doing and why, and record the call (Module 6). In New Zealand the Insurance Council tells policyholders to contact their insurer before work is done, so check the owner has.
  2. Power and electronics. The fire started in the switchboard cupboard, so nothing is powered until an electrician has made the board safe. The point-of-sale terminals are unplugged where they stand, photographed, labelled and set aside for a specialist.
  3. Bare metal first. Wipe residue off the stainless benches and chrome tapware with the method your test patch chose, starting with the surfaces nearest the fire. Record the start time against each item.
  4. Humidity. At 80 %RH, dehumidification goes in as soon as an electrician-confirmed circuit is available. Close the room so the dehumidifier dries the kitchen, not the street.

Common mistakes

  • Waiting for the full scope before touching metal. Corrosion keeps going while the paperwork moves.
  • Powering a terminal “just to back up the sales data”. That is a job for the owner’s IT provider or an electronics specialist; a powered, contaminated board can become a total loss.
  • Propping the doors open to air the kitchen when the outside air is as humid as the inside. The dehumidifier then works on the weather instead of the room.

See it

The diagram shows the three drivers of corrosion and the mitigation step that answers each.

Do it in metric

Check what dehumidifying the air alone achieves. At 26 °C and 80 %RH the air holds about 17.0 g of water per kg of dry air; at 26 °C and 50 %RH, about 10.5 g/kg. The kitchen is 6.0 m × 4.5 m × 2.7 m = 72.9 m³, roughly 86 kg of air at about 1.18 kg/m³. Taking 6.5 g/kg out of 86 kg of air removes only about 0.56 kg of water — a little over half a litre. The air dries quickly; the wet materials keep feeding it, so the dehumidifier runs, and you keep logging °C and %RH, until the readings hold.

Field download

The Corrosion, contents and HVAC triage sheet has a corrosion-priority list (electronics, bare metal, chrome, tools) with start time, action and result columns, and an air log in °C, %RH and g/kg.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks why acid residue matters, what humidity does to corrosion, and why you never power up contaminated electronics.

Takeaway

Smoke residue corrodes metal, faster when it is humid and worse with time. Clean metal early, bring the humidity down, isolate electronics and record it all. Next lesson: contents and the HVAC system.

Sources for this lesson

  • Cider L. Reconditioning surface mount electronics after smoke contamination. IVF report 92/20, 1992 (NIST FireDOC abstract). Read 02/11/2026.
  • Liu X et al. Corrosive effects of smoke with different concentrations from PVC on 304 stainless steel and 6061 aluminium alloy. Corros Eng Sci Technol 2018. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Hirschler MM, Smith GF. Corrosivity of smoke towards metals. J Vinyl Technol 1989. Read 02/11/2026.
  • Insurance Council of New Zealand, Making a claim. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Contents triage and the HVAC system
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Triage categories and HVAC rules are CARSI method wording flagged for SME verification. Item counts are illustrative.

On the job

A family home in Palmerston North had a lounge fire. The ducted heat pump ran for an hour after the fire because nobody turned it off. The bedrooms at the far end of the house have soot on the ceiling around every outlet, and the owners want to know what of their belongings can be saved.

The idea

Contents triage. CARSI sorts every affected item into one of three groups before anything is cleaned or moved:

  • Restore on site — light residue on a durable surface that can be cleaned in place with the method its residue and material call for.
  • Restore off site — items needing specialist cleaning, deodorisation or repair in a controlled facility: textiles, artwork, documents, electronics.
  • Total loss — too damaged, too porous or too contaminated to restore economically or safely. Heavily affected food, cosmetics and medicines are discarded.

Photograph and inventory every item before it is moved or cleaned, with its room and its group. That inventory is the backbone of the contents claim and the record the owner will check against. Keep restorable items in a clean, controlled area away from cleaned structure, packed so odour does not transfer from item to item. Items with sentimental value are a conversation with the owner, not only a cost decision.

The HVAC system. A ducted system that ran during or after a fire is one of the fastest ways residue reaches rooms the fire never touched (Module 2). Assess it as part of the structure:

  • supply and return outlets, for soot around and inside them;
  • filters, which usually show contamination even when rooms look clean;
  • the coil, fan and the inside of the ductwork, especially after wet or fuel-oil residue;
  • whether it ran during or after the fire, which raises the chance of whole-house contamination.

Keep a contaminated system switched off and isolated until it has been professionally cleaned and its filters replaced. Running it re-contaminates rooms you have already cleaned. Seal outlets in cleaned rooms while work continues elsewhere, and record the system’s condition and any referral to a duct-cleaning or HVAC contractor in the job file. Work on the refrigeration and electrical parts of the system is for licensed trades.

Worked scenario: the cooler that ran through the smoke

(Illustrative.) Back to the bushfire-affected house near Cobargo from Module 2. The evaporative cooler ran for two days in heavy smoke, its ducts serve every room, and with hot weather coming the owners want to turn it back on.

Decision point. The cooler stays off. A system that drew smoky air through the house for two days was the main route the residue took, and running it before it is cleaned blows residue from the ducts across rooms you have already cleaned. EPA Victoria’s ash guidance says to have heating, ventilating and air-conditioning units and all ductwork professionally cleaned, and filters replaced, to remove soot, ash and smoke residue. Refer the cooler and its ducts to a contractor and record the referral. If the family needs cooling in the meantime, discuss options for a cleaned room with them; it is not a reason to restart the ducts.

Contents on a bushfire job. Curtains, bedding and upholstery carry the same fine ash as the surfaces. EPA Victoria advises washing soft furnishings or vacuuming them with a HEPA-filtered vacuum so particles do not blow back into the house. Triage still applies: light ash on durable items is restored on site; heavily affected textiles and anything with a strong odour go off site, or are written off with the owner’s agreement and a photograph.

Common mistakes with contents and HVAC

  • Moving contents before they are photographed and inventoried.
  • Packing smoky textiles in the same carton as clean ones, so odour transfers.
  • Replacing the filter and restarting the system without cleaning the ducts behind it.
  • Vacuuming ash with a household vacuum. Without a HEPA filter, the finest particles blow straight back into the room.

See it

The diagram shows the three contents groups and the four HVAC checks, both starting from the photo inventory.

Do it in metric

The Palmerston North inventory (illustrative) records 140 items: 82 restore on site, 38 restore off site and 20 total loss. As shares: 82 ÷ 140 ≈ 59 %, 38 ÷ 140 ≈ 27 %, 20 ÷ 140 ≈ 14 %. The ducted system has eight outlets and a 600 mm × 600 mm return filter, 0.36 m² of filter face. Record each outlet’s condition on the floor plan and photograph the filter before it is removed.

Field download

The Corrosion, contents and HVAC triage sheet includes a contents log (item, room, group, photo reference) and an HVAC checklist with an isolation sign-off.

Check yourself

The Module 5 check asks you to triage items into the three groups and explain why a contaminated HVAC system stays off.

Takeaway

Photograph and inventory first, triage every item into one of three groups, and keep a contaminated HVAC system off until it is cleaned. Next module: odour control, verification and the job file.

lessons.title: Odour control: source first, devices last
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Odour-control sequence is CARSI method wording flagged for SME verification. Ozone and hydroxyl statements follow the CARSI Ozone and Hydroxyl Generators course.

On the job

The Wollongong unit from Module 1 has been cleaned, but the bedroom still smells of smoke. The insurer’s builder suggests “just running the ozone machine overnight”, with the tenant due back the next morning. Two things are wrong with that plan, and they are the same two things this lesson is about.

The idea

Odour is residue. Smoke odour comes from particles and odour-causing compounds left in and on materials. Deodorising works only after the source has been removed and the surfaces cleaned; a product or machine that masks a source still in the room hides the problem until the weather warms up or the humidity rises. CARSI’s odour-control sequence is:

  1. Remove the source: charred and saturated materials out (Module 4).
  2. Clean every reachable surface, including cavities, roof space and the HVAC system.
  3. Seal porous surfaces that cannot be fully cleaned, such as charred framing, with a suitable sealer, so remaining compounds are locked in rather than released.
  4. Treat remaining odour with a method matched to the space and whether people are present.
  5. Verify and record the result before any cavity is closed or the occupants return.

Ozone. Ozone is a workplace hazard with an exposure limit in both countries. In Australia ozone has a peak limitation of 0.1 ppm (0.2 mg/m³): the maximum a worker can be exposed to, measured over no more than 15 minutes. In New Zealand the workplace exposure standard for ozone is a ceiling of 0.1 ppm (0.2 mg/m³), a concentration not to be exceeded at any time. The number is the same either side of the Tasman. Consistent with the CARSI Ozone and Hydroxyl Generators course: ozone treatment is for an empty, isolated space only, with people and pets out, entries signed and secured, plants, rubber and susceptible fabrics protected, and a calibrated ozone meter used to measure rather than assume. The worker limit is not a clearance level for occupants; when people may go back in is a site-specific decision based on the manufacturer’s instructions and measured readings.

Hydroxyl generators. Do not treat a hydroxyl unit as safe to run with people inside because it is “not an ozone machine”. A 2021 study of a commercial hydroxyl radical generator in an office measured organic acids and new particles forming while it ran. The CARSI Ozone course found no source showing how well these units remove odour on Australian restoration jobs, and it recommends keeping people out until you know what your unit produces. Ask the supplier for an independent test report.

Back to Wollongong. A tenant due back in the morning rules out an overnight ozone run. The bedroom smell says a source or a missed surface remains: re-survey, clean, seal if needed, and only then consider a device treatment scheduled for when the unit can be empty.

Decision points: odour in a bushfire-affected house

(Illustrative.) The Cobargo house has been cleaned top to bottom and the cooler is off, waiting for its contractor. A faint smoke smell remains in the main bedroom. The owner has bought an odour absorber and a negative ion generator and asks whether they will finish the job.

  • What those devices do not do. NSW Health says humidifiers, negative ion generators and odour absorbers do not remove fine particles in bushfire smoke. If fine residue remains, a device will not take it away; cleaning will.
  • Where is it coming from? Re-survey the bedroom against the five pathways: the cooler outlet in the ceiling, the curtains, the mattress, the top of the wardrobe. A smell that is strongest at the outlet points to the ducts, not the room.
  • Can a device treatment go ahead? Only after the source is found and cleaned, and only with a method matched to the space: ozone in an empty, isolated house, measured with a calibrated meter, never with the family sleeping in it.

Common mistakes with odour

  • Treating odour before the source is removed, so the smell returns on the first hot day.
  • Running a hydroxyl unit with people inside because it is “not an ozone machine”.
  • Recording “odour gone” instead of who assessed it, where and when.
  • Painting a sealer over a surface that has not been verified clean, which locks residue in under the paint.

See it

The five steps run in order, and each one only works if the step before it is done. The note underneath is the ozone rule that trips crews up most often.

Do it in metric

The bedroom is 3.4 m × 3.1 m with a 2.4 m ceiling: 10.5 m² and about 25.3 m³. If an ozone treatment is scheduled for later, the plan states that volume, the unit’s make, model and setting, the start and stop times, the meter and its calibration date, and readings logged in ppm against the 0.1 ppm worker limit before anyone enters. A reading is a number with a time beside it, not “smell gone”.

Field download

The Odour control and job file checklist takes you through the five-step sequence, with an ozone isolation and readings log.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks you to order the odour-control steps, state the ozone limits in Australia and New Zealand, and decide whether a device treatment can go ahead.

Takeaway

Odour is residue: remove it, clean it, seal it, and only then treat what remains, with the space empty for ozone. Measure, do not assume. Next lesson: verification and the job file.

Sources for this lesson

  • WorkSafe Victoria, Ozone exposure safety alert (3 February 2025). Read 02/11/2026.
  • WorkSafe New Zealand, Workplace exposure standards: ozone. Read 02/11/2026.
  • CARSI, Ozone and Hydroxyl Generators on Restoration Jobs: What the Evidence Says (CARSI course, sources read 14/10/2026).
  • Joo T et al. Formation of oxidized gases and secondary organic aerosol from a commercial oxidant-generating electronic air cleaner. Environ Sci Technol Lett 2021;8(8):691-698. Read 02/11/2026.
  • NSW Health, Protect yourself from bushfire smoke. Read 02/11/2026.

lessons.title: Verification, the job file and the insurance context
lessons.contentBody:
DRAFT for SME review. Prices are illustrative AUD figures flagged for verification.

On the job

Six weeks after a fire in a Hobart home, the owner tells the insurer the house still smells and the kitchen ceiling has “come up brown” after repainting. The insurer asks the restorer for the job file. One restorer can show the boundary sketch, the residue tests, the clean and seal records, the odour readings and a signed handover. Another has a few phone photos and an invoice. Only one of them can answer the complaint.

The idea

Verify before you hand over. Before cavities are closed, sealers are painted over or occupants return, check the work against the scope: surfaces clean to the touch and the eye, odour assessed room by room by someone who has not been working in it all day, moisture readings at the dry goal where the building was wet, the HVAC system cleaned or isolated with a referral, and asbestos clearance on file where it applied. Record who checked, when and what they found. If an area fails, it goes back to cleaning, not to the painter.

Build the job file as you work. Records made at the time are stronger than ones reconstructed later. The file holds: the site release and make-safe record; the boundary sketch and survey; hazardous-materials findings, reports and clearances; residue tests and cleaning records; corrosion actions with times; the contents inventory; the HVAC record; odour-control steps and device readings; moisture readings; scope changes and who approved them; and the handover. Date and time every entry, and keep the photos linked to the room and the step.

The insurance context. Most fire restoration in both countries happens inside an insurance claim. In Australia, insurers that subscribe to the General Insurance Code of Practice commit to its standards, including timeframes for claims, and if a service supplier acting for the insurer does not comply with the Code, the insurer is in breach. In New Zealand, members of the Insurance Council of New Zealand are bound by the Fair Insurance Code, under which the insurer acknowledges a claim within 5 business days and decides within 10 business days of having the information it needs. The ICNZ also tells policyholders to contact their insurer before having any work done. For the restorer that means: get scope approval before work beyond emergency mitigation, record what was approved and by whom, and keep the insured event separate from pre-existing damage. Whether something is covered is the insurer’s decision, not yours.

Consumer law. Your services carry statutory guarantees in both countries. In Australia, under the Australian Consumer Law, services must be provided with an acceptable level of care and skill and be fit for any stated purpose. In New Zealand, under the Consumer Guarantees Act 1993, services must be carried out with reasonable care and skill and be fit for purpose. A defensible job file is how you show you met them.

Field walk-through: handing over the Townsville kitchen

(Illustrative.) The commercial kitchen from Module 5 is ready to reopen. Walk the verification the way the insurer’s assessor will.

  1. Surfaces. Wipe-test benches, canopy and tapware with a clean white cloth, and record the result area by area, not “kitchen OK”.
  2. Odour. Someone who has not been working in the kitchen walks it and records what they smell, and where.
  3. Air and moisture. The final °C and %RH readings are on file beside the dehumidifier log.
  4. Electronics and the board. The electrician’s sign-off on the switchboard and the specialist’s report on the terminals are in the file. Nothing was powered without them.
  5. Scope. Every item beyond emergency mitigation has an approval beside it: who approved it, when, and how.

Common mistakes in the job file

  • Photos without rooms, dates or steps. A photo nobody can place proves nothing.
  • Rebuilding the file from memory at the end of the job.
  • Mixing pre-existing damage into the fire claim. If the canopy was rusted before the fire, the photos and the file should say so.
  • Handing over with an open item, such as an HVAC referral not yet done, without writing it into the handover.

See it

The timeline shows each stage adding its own records, so the file is complete at handover rather than assembled afterwards.

Do it in metric

Price the Hobart clean-and-seal stage in AUD. CARSI prices in Australian dollars. Suppose (illustrative) the stage is A$3,850 excluding GST. Australian GST is 10 %, so the GST is A$385 and the price is A$4,235 including GST. The scope covers 128 m² of wall and ceiling, so A$3,850 ÷ 128 ≈ A$30.08 per m² excluding GST. Show the area, the rate and the GST separately so the insurer’s assessor can check each one.

Field download

The Odour control and job file checklist ends with the verification checklist and a job file index for Australian and New Zealand claims.

Check yourself

The Module 6 check asks what goes in the job file, what verification means before handover, and how the consumer guarantees apply in each country. The final knowledge check follows; as with every module check and the practical task, the pass mark is 80 %.

Takeaway

Verify before you hand over, build the file as you go, get approval before you go beyond mitigation, and price it so an assessor can follow it. That completes the teaching. The practical task asks you to do all of it on one job.
